recipes.name: Birria Tacos
recipes.description: Slow-braised beef stewed in a rich red chile broth until fall-apart tender, served in corn tortillas dipped in the consommé and crisped on a hot comal. Served with a cup of the deeply flavored broth for dipping.

ingredients.name: dried guajillo chiles, stemmed and seeded
dried ancho chiles, stemmed and seeded

instructions: Toast the dried guajillo, ancho, and árbol chiles in a dry skillet over medium heat for 30 seconds per side until fragrant. Transfer to a pot, cover with water, add the tomatoes, half the onion, and 3 garlic cloves. Bring to a boil, then simmer 10 minutes until the chiles are softened.

Transfer the softened chiles and vegetables to a blender with 1 cup of the chile-soaking water, beef broth, vinegar, remaining garlic, cumin, oregano, cinnamon, cloves, peppercorns, and salt. Blend on high until completely smooth, then strain through a fine-mesh sieve.

Season the beef generously with salt and pepper. Heat a Dutch oven or heavy pot over medium-high heat with a drizzle of oil. Working in batches, sear the beef on all sides until deeply browned, about 3-4 minutes per side. Remove and set aside.

Pour the blended chile sauce over the seared beef in the pot. Add bay leaves and enough water so the beef is submerged. Bring to a boil, then reduce heat to low, cover, and braise for 3 to 3.5 hours until the meat is completely fork-tender and falling apart.

Remove the beef and shred it with two forks, discarding any bones. Reserve the braising liquid as the consommé. Skim the red chile fat that rises to the top of the consommé and reserve it in a shallow bowl for dipping the tortillas.

Heat a comal or flat griddle over medium-high heat. Quickly dip a corn tortilla into the shallow bowl of chile fat and lay it flat on the hot comal. Add a handful of shredded Oaxaca cheese and 2-3 tablespoons of shredded birria beef to one half. Fold the tortilla over and cook 1-2 minutes per side until crispy and golden with a deep red color.
Ladle the warm consommé into small cups. Serve the tacos immediately garnished with diced onion and cilantro, with lime wedges and a cup of consommé alongside for dipping.

recipes.name: Al Pastor Tacos
recipes.description: Thinly sliced marinated pork cooked on a vertical spit (trompo) in an achiote-guajillo adobo, shaved off and served on small corn tortillas with a slice of grilled pineapple. A Mexico City institution born from Lebanese shawarma tradition.

ingredients.name: boneless pork shoulder, sliced thin (1/4 inch)
dried guajillo chiles, stemmed and seeded
dried ancho chile, stemmed and seeded

instructions: Toast the guajillo and ancho chiles in a dry skillet over medium heat for about 30 seconds per side until fragrant and slightly puffed. Transfer to a bowl, cover with boiling water, and soak for 20 minutes until softened.

Drain the chiles and transfer to a blender with the chipotle, achiote paste, pineapple juice, vinegar, garlic, onion, cumin, oregano, black pepper, and salt. Blend on high until completely smooth to form the adobo marinade.
Place the thinly sliced pork in a large bowl or zip-lock bag and pour the adobo over it. Toss well to coat every slice. Cover and refrigerate for at least 4 hours, preferably overnight.

When ready to cook, remove the pork from the marinade. For home cooking: heat a large cast-iron skillet or griddle over high heat. Cook the pork slices in a single layer for 3-4 minutes per side until caramelized and cooked through. Grill the pineapple slices alongside until charred.
Once cooked, use a knife or scissors to roughly chop the pork and pineapple into small pieces on the cutting board.
Warm the tortillas on the same hot skillet or comal, about 30 seconds per side. For each taco, use two tortillas stacked on top of each other for structural support.
Fill each double-stacked tortilla with a generous spoonful of al pastor, add a few pineapple pieces, and garnish with diced onion and cilantro. Serve immediately with salsa verde and lime wedges.

recipes.name: Carnitas
recipes.description: Pork slow-cooked in a copper pot (cazo) full of lard until meltingly tender on the inside and caramelized and crispy on the outside. The secret of Michoacán is the addition of orange, Mexican Coke, and lard for an unbeatable depth of flavor.

ingredients.name: bone-in pork shoulder, cut into large chunks

instructions: Melt the lard in a large heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven (ideally a copper cazo) over medium-high heat. The pot should be large enough to hold all the pork comfortably.
Add the pork chunks to the hot lard in a single layer. The lard should come up about halfway on the pork. Fry, turning occasionally, for about 20 minutes until the outsides are browned.
In a cup, dissolve 1.5 tablespoons of salt into 1 cup of water to make a salt brine. Once the pork is browned, reduce the heat to medium-low.

Add the Coca-Cola, the salt brine, squeezed orange halves (drop the entire squeezed orange in), onion, garlic, bay leaves, cloves, and peppercorns directly into the lard with the pork. The liquid will sizzle aggressively.
Bring to a gentle simmer, cover, and cook on low heat for 1.5 to 2 hours, turning the pork occasionally, until the meat is completely tender and pulls apart easily with a fork.

Remove the lid and increase heat to medium-high for the final 20-30 minutes to let the remaining liquid evaporate and the pork caramelize and become crispy on all sides. Watch carefully to prevent burning.

Remove the pork with a slotted spoon, letting excess lard drip off. Transfer to a cutting board and roughly chop or pull apart the meat. Warm tortillas on the comal and serve the carnitas with toppings.

recipes.name: Red Pozole
recipes.description: A hearty, ancient ceremonial stew from Guerrero featuring large-kernel hominy corn and braised pork in a deep red dried-chile broth. Served with a lavish table of crunchy garnishes that each guest adds to their own bowl.

ingredients.name: dried guajillo chiles, stemmed and seeded
dried ancho chiles, stemmed and seeded

instructions: Place the pork shoulder and trotters in a large pot. Cover with cold water (about 4 quarts). Bring to a boil, skimming any foam that rises. Add half the onion, 3 garlic cloves, bay leaves, and 1 tablespoon salt. Reduce to a low simmer, cover, and cook for 1.5 to 2 hours until the pork is very tender.
While the pork cooks, toast the guajillo, ancho, and árbol chiles in a dry skillet for 30 seconds per side. Transfer to a bowl, cover with boiling water, and soak 20 minutes until soft.
Transfer the softened chiles to a blender with 1 cup of their soaking liquid, the remaining onion, garlic, cumin, and oregano. Blend on high until completely smooth. Strain through a fine sieve.
Remove the cooked pork from the broth and let it cool slightly. Shred the meat, discarding bones and skin. Strain the pork broth and return it to the pot.
Heat a tablespoon of oil in a skillet over medium-high heat. Add the blended chile sauce and fry, stirring constantly, for 5 minutes until it darkens and thickens slightly.

Add the chile sauce and the drained hominy to the pork broth. Bring to a boil, then simmer on medium heat for 30-40 minutes until the hominy is tender and has absorbed the flavor of the broth. Add the shredded pork back to the pot. Adjust salt.
Ladle the pozole into deep bowls with plenty of hominy and pork. Set out all the garnishes in small bowls and let each guest pile on their own toppings. Serve with tostadas on the side.

recipes.name: Cochinita Pibil
recipes.description: Yucatecan slow-roasted pork marinated in achiote and bitter orange juice, wrapped in banana leaves and cooked until meltingly tender. Originally cooked in an underground pit (pib), this is one of Mexico's most ancient and iconic dishes.

ingredients.name: boneless pork shoulder, cut into 3-inch pieces
banana leaves, cut into large pieces

instructions: Combine the achiote paste, orange juice, lime juice, vinegar, garlic, onion, cumin, oregano, and salt in a blender. Blend on high until the marinade is completely smooth and uniform.

Place the pork pieces in a large bowl or baking dish and pour the achiote marinade over them. Toss until every piece is well coated. Cover and refrigerate for at least 6 hours, or ideally overnight for maximum flavor.

Preheat your oven to 325°F (160°C). Pass the banana leaves briefly over a gas flame or hot comal for a few seconds until they turn bright green and become pliable. This makes them flexible and brings out their aroma.
Line a Dutch oven or deep baking dish with the banana leaves, letting them drape over the sides. Pour the marinated pork and all the marinade juices into the center.
Fold the banana leaves up over the pork to completely enclose it. Cover tightly with a lid or foil. Roast for 3 to 3.5 hours until the pork is completely pull-apart tender.
Remove from the oven and let rest 15 minutes. Pull the pork apart into shreds directly in the cooking vessel, mixing it with the orange-achiote juices that have accumulated.
Warm the tortillas on a hot comal. Serve the cochinita pibil on the tortillas topped with pickled red onions with habanero, a drizzle of habanero salsa, and a squeeze of lime.

recipes.name: Pork Tamales
recipes.spanishName: Tamales de Puerco en Chile Rojo
recipes.description: A cornerstone of Mexican cooking, tamales are masa dough filled with slow-cooked pork in red chile sauce, wrapped in dried corn husks and steamed until the masa is perfectly tender. A communal dish traditionally made in large batches for celebrations.

ingredients.name: dried guajillo chiles, stemmed and seeded
dried ancho chiles, stemmed and seeded

instructions: Place the dried corn husks in a large bowl or pot of very hot water. Soak for at least 30 minutes, weighing them down with a plate so they are fully submerged, until completely softened and pliable.

Make the chile sauce for the filling: Toast the guajillo and ancho chiles briefly in a dry skillet, soak in boiling water 20 minutes, then blend with garlic, cumin, 1 cup of soaking water, and salt until smooth. Strain through a sieve. Toss the shredded pork with the sauce in a skillet over medium heat for 5 minutes. Set aside to cool.

Make the masa dough: Using a stand or hand mixer, beat the lard on medium-high speed for 3-5 minutes until light and fluffy. In a separate bowl, mix the masa harina, baking powder, and salt. Add the dry ingredients to the lard alternately with warm broth, mixing until a soft, pliable dough forms. It should be like thick peanut butter. Test a small ball in water—if it floats, it is ready.

Spread masa: Lay a soaked corn husk on a flat surface with the wide end toward you. Using the back of a spoon, spread about 3 tablespoons of masa dough into a thin, even rectangle (about 4x5 inches), leaving a 1-inch border on all sides.
Add filling: Place 2-3 tablespoons of the pork filling in a line down the center of the masa. Do not overfill.

Fold and tie: Fold one long side of the husk over the filling so the masa edges meet, then fold the other side over. Fold the bottom (narrow) end of the husk up. Tear a thin strip of husk and tie around the tamal to keep it closed. Repeat until all the masa and filling is used.

Steam the tamales: Stand the tamales upright, open end up, in a large steamer basket. Cover with extra corn husks or a damp cloth to trap steam. Fill the steamer with water, bring to a boil, then steam on medium heat for 1 hour to 1 hour 15 minutes, checking water level frequently and refilling as needed. The tamales are done when the masa pulls cleanly away from the husk.

recipes.name: Stuffed Poblano Peppers
recipes.description: Roasted poblano peppers stuffed with Oaxaca or Monterey Jack cheese, dipped in a light, cloud-like beaten egg batter, and fried golden. Served over a savory tomato-chipotle ranchera sauce. A Puebla classic and one of the most beloved dishes in all of Mexico.

ingredients.name: Oaxaca or Monterey Jack cheese, in strips

instructions: Roast the poblanos: Place peppers on a foil-lined baking sheet and broil 4-6 inches from the heat, turning occasionally, for 10-12 minutes total until all sides are blackened and blistered. Immediately transfer to a bowl, cover tightly with plastic wrap, and let steam for 10 minutes. This loosens the skin.

Peel, slit, and stuff: Gently rub off the charred skins under running water. Use a small knife to make a single lengthwise slit in each pepper. Carefully remove the seeds and membranes through the slit, keeping the stem intact. Stuff each pepper generously with cheese strips, then press the slit closed.

Make the ranchera sauce: Blend the tomatoes, onion, garlic, and chipotle together until smooth. Heat 1 tablespoon oil in a saucepan over medium-high heat, add the tomato sauce and fry for 5 minutes, stirring, until it darkens. Add the broth and oregano, simmer 10 minutes. Season with salt.

Make the egg batter: Using a hand mixer or stand mixer, beat the egg whites in a clean bowl on high speed until stiff glossy peaks form. Add the egg yolks one at a time, beating on low speed just until incorporated. Season with a pinch of salt.
Dredge the peppers: Roll each stuffed pepper in flour, shaking off excess so it is lightly and evenly coated on all sides. The flour coating helps the egg batter stick.

Fry the chiles: Heat about 2 inches of oil in a deep skillet over medium-high heat to 350°F (175°C). Holding each pepper by the stem, dip into the egg batter, coating all sides. Gently slide into the hot oil. Fry 2-3 minutes per side until golden and puffy. Drain on paper towels.
Serve the chiles rellenos immediately on a pool of warm ranchera sauce, topped with a drizzle of Mexican crema and crumbled queso fresco.

recipes.name: Green Enchiladas
recipes.description: Corn tortillas filled with shredded chicken, rolled up and smothered in a vibrant, roasted tomatillo salsa verde, then topped with crema, queso fresco, and onion. A bright, tangy counterpart to the more common red enchilada.

ingredients.name: boneless chicken breast or thighs, boiled and shredded

instructions: Make the salsa verde: Place the tomatillos, serranos, jalapeño, onion, and garlic on a foil-lined baking sheet. Broil 4-5 inches from heat for 5-7 minutes until the tomatillos are charred and blistered, turning once. Let cool slightly.
Transfer the roasted vegetables to a blender. Add the cilantro and chicken broth. Blend until smooth. Season with salt.

Heat 1 tablespoon of oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat. Pour in the blended salsa verde and fry, stirring frequently, for 5 minutes until it darkens slightly and thickens. This step is critical for developing deep flavor. Remove from heat.
Toss the shredded chicken with a ladleful of the salsa verde in a bowl, so it is moist and well-seasoned.

Heat the remaining oil in a small skillet over medium heat. Pass each corn tortilla through the hot oil for about 5 seconds per side — just enough to soften it without making it crispy. This prevents the tortilla from cracking when rolled.
Place about 2-3 tablespoons of chicken filling in each softened tortilla, roll it up tightly, and place seam-side down in a baking dish. Repeat with all tortillas, arranging them snugly side by side.

Pour the remaining salsa verde over the rolled enchiladas, making sure to coat them all. Top with queso fresco, a generous drizzle of crema, sliced onion, and cilantro. Serve immediately (or bake at 350°F for 10 minutes if you prefer them warm and bubbly).

recipes.name: Tripe and Hominy Soup
recipes.description: A deeply restorative and bold northern Mexican soup made with tender beef tripe, hominy corn, and a red guajillo-ancho chile broth cooked low and slow for hours. Traditionally eaten on weekend mornings and celebrated as a hangover cure.

ingredients.name: beef tripe (honeycomb preferred), cleaned and cut into 2-inch pieces
dried guajillo chiles, stemmed and seeded
dried ancho chile, stemmed and seeded

instructions: Pre-clean the tripe: Place the tripe in a large pot, cover with cold water, bring to a boil and cook for 5 minutes. Drain, rinse the tripe under cold water, and repeat this process once more. This removes impurities and tones down the strong smell.

Start the broth: In a large stockpot, combine the cleaned tripe, beef bones, half the onion, 4 garlic cloves, and bay leaves. Cover with about 4 quarts of water. Bring to a boil, skim any foam, reduce heat to low, cover, and cook for 3-4 hours until the tripe is completely tender when pierced with a fork.

Make the chile base: Toast the guajillo and ancho chiles in a dry skillet for 30 seconds per side. Soak in boiling water 20 minutes. Blend with the remaining onion, garlic, cumin, and 1 cup of soaking water until smooth. Strain through a sieve.

Heat a tablespoon of oil in a skillet over high heat. Add the blended chile sauce and fry, stirring constantly, for 5 minutes until it turns a darker, deeper red. This step fries off the raw chile flavor.
Once the tripe is tender, remove the bones. Add the fried chile sauce and the drained hominy to the pot. Stir to combine, then add oregano and salt.
Simmer uncovered over medium heat for another 30-45 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the hominy has bloomed (opened up like flowers), the broth is richly flavored and deeply red.
Ladle into large, deep bowls making sure each serving has plenty of tripe and hominy. Serve immediately with all garnishes on the side in small bowls so guests can customize their bowl.

recipes.name: Sopes
recipes.description: Thick, hand-pinched masa discs cooked on a comal and then fried lightly to give them a slight crust. The raised edges hold a cargo of refried beans and toppings. A fixture at street markets across Mexico.
instructions: Make the masa: In a large bowl, combine masa harina, salt, and warm water. Mix with your hands, kneading for 2-3 minutes until you have a smooth, pliable dough similar to play-doh. If the dough is dry and cracking at the edges, add water one tablespoon at a time. If sticky, add a touch more masa harina.
Divide the dough into 12 equal balls, each about the size of a large golf ball. Keep covered with a damp cloth to prevent drying out.

Heat a dry comal or cast-iron skillet over medium heat. Using a tortilla press or heavy skillet, press each dough ball between two sheets of plastic wrap to form a disc about 1/4 inch thick and 4 inches across — much thicker than a regular tortilla.
Cook each sope on the dry comal for 2 minutes per side until lightly spotted and firm. Work in batches.

While each sope is still warm and pliable (this is important — work quickly!), use your fingers to pinch and press the edges up all around the disc to form a raised rim, like a tiny shallow bowl. This rim holds the toppings in place. Set aside.
Heat the oil in a skillet over medium-high heat. Lightly fry each sope, flat bottom down, for 1-2 minutes until slightly crisped and golden. Drain on paper towels.

Assemble immediately: Spread a generous tablespoon of warm refried beans onto each sope, add a spoonful of chicken tinga, and finish with shredded lettuce, crumbled queso fresco, a drizzle of crema, and your choice of salsa. Serve at once.

recipes.name: Oaxacan Pizza
recipes.description: A massive, partially dried and crisped corn tortilla (about 12-14 inches) spread with smoky asiento (unrefined lard), creamy black beans, ribbons of stretchy quesillo cheese, and meat. Often called the Oaxacan pizza, it is the crown jewel of Oaxacan street food.

ingredients.name: large tlayuda tortillas (or large corn tortillas), 12-14 inches
asiento (unrefined pork lard) or refried black beans as substitute
quesillo (Oaxacan string cheese), pulled into strips
tasajo (dried beef) or cecina or chorizo

instructions: Prepare the tortilla base: Place the large corn tortilla on a hot comal or grill over medium heat. Toast it for 3-4 minutes per side until it starts to firm up and develops light char spots — it should be semi-crunchy but still pliable enough to fold if desired.
Spread the asiento: Remove from the comal and immediately spread a thin layer of asiento (or substitute with refried beans) across the entire surface of the tortilla while it is still hot.
Add the beans: Spread the refried black beans in a thick, even layer over the asiento. The beans should cover the entire surface, right up to the edges.
Add the cheese: Lay the pulled quesillo strings evenly across the beans. Return the tlayuda to the comal over medium-low heat and cook for 2-3 minutes until the cheese begins to melt and turn gooey.

Cook the meat: While the cheese melts, cook the tasajo, cecina, or chorizo separately on the comal or in a skillet over high heat. Tasajo and cecina need 2-3 minutes per side. Slice or crumble and set aside.
Add fresh toppings: Scatter the shredded cabbage over the melted cheese. Add the sliced tomato and avocado. Squeeze fresh lime over the vegetables.
Place the cooked meat on top. Serve flat or folded in half, open-faced style. Drizzle with salsa and serve with additional lime wedges.

recipes.name: Basket Tacos
recipes.description: Also called tacos sudados (sweaty tacos), these are soft corn tortillas stuffed with fillings like chicharrón prensado, refried beans, or potato-chorizo, then stacked in an oil-bathed basket and left to steam for an hour. A beloved Mexico City morning street food eaten for breakfast.

ingredients.name: dried guajillo chiles, toasted and rehydrated

instructions: Prepare the fillings: Mix the cooked chorizo with the diced boiled potatoes in a bowl and season with salt. Keep the chicharrón prensado and refried beans in separate bowls. You now have three fillings.

Assemble the tacos: Warm a stack of tortillas briefly on the comal until softened. Add a small amount (about 2 tablespoons) of one filling to the center of each tortilla. Fold in half. These should be compact — not overstuffed.

Make the aromatic oil: Blend the rehydrated guajillo chiles, garlic, and a pinch of salt with 2 tablespoons of water until smooth. Heat the vegetable oil in a small saucepan over medium heat. Fry the chile paste in the oil for 2-3 minutes, stirring constantly, until fragrant and the oil turns a deep red. Remove from heat.

Layer the basket: Line a large basket (or a stock pot) with a plastic bag, then a kitchen towel. Arrange a layer of assembled tacos in the basket. Scatter sliced onion over the layer. Repeat, building layers until all tacos are in the basket.
Pour the hot aromatic red oil evenly over all the tacos so it seeps down through all the layers. This oil is the key to the unique steamed flavor.

Seal the basket: Close the kitchen towel tightly over the tacos, then seal the plastic bag. Let the tacos rest and steam in the sealed basket for at least 45 minutes to 1 hour. The steam softens them and melds the flavors.
Serve from the basket: The tacos should be soft, slightly damp with oil, and intensely flavorful. Serve with salsa verde, salsa roja, and pickled jalapeños on the side.

recipes.name: Mexican Stuffed Corn Cakes
recipes.description: Thick, round masa cakes cooked on a comal then split open and stuffed with savory fillings. The name means 'little fatties' — a term of endearment. Popular at markets and street stalls across the center and north of Mexico, with endless regional filling variations.

ingredients.name: chicharrón en salsa verde (pork rind in green sauce)

instructions: Prepare the masa: In a bowl, mix masa harina, salt, and lard (if using). Add warm water gradually, kneading until you achieve a smooth, soft dough. Pinch a small piece — it should not crack at the edges. If it does, add a little more water. Cover with a damp cloth.

Shape the gorditas: Divide the dough into 8 equal portions. Roll each into a ball, then flatten between your palms into a disc about 1/2 inch thick and 4 inches in diameter. They should be noticeably thicker than a tortilla.

Cook on the comal: Heat a dry comal or cast-iron skillet over medium heat. Cook the gorditas for 3-4 minutes per side until firm and lightly spotted with brown. They should not be raw inside. The inside should steam through from the comal heat. Press lightly with a spatula if needed.

Optional light fry: For a slightly crispier exterior, heat a thin film of oil in a skillet over medium-high heat and fry each gordita for 1 minute per side until lightly golden. Drain on paper towels.

Make the chicharrón filling: In a small pot, heat a tablespoon of oil over medium heat. Add salsa verde and chicharrón pieces. Cook, stirring, for 5-8 minutes until the chicharrón softens and absorbs the salsa. Season with salt.

Split and fill: Using a knife, carefully split each gordita along one edge to open a pocket inside, like a pita bread. Be gentle — don't cut all the way through. Spread a little refried beans inside, then add a generous spoonful of chicharrón en salsa verde.
Top with crumbled queso fresco, a drizzle of crema, shredded lettuce, and salsa roja. Serve immediately.

recipes.name: Mexican Street Corn
recipes.description: Whole corn on the cob grilled or boiled until charred and smoky, then impaled on a stick and lavishly dressed with mayonnaise, cotija cheese, chile powder, and lime. An unmissable sight at every Mexican street fair, market, and park.
instructions: Grill the corn: Preheat a grill or grill pan to high heat. Place the husked corn directly on the grates and cook, turning every 2-3 minutes, for 10-12 minutes total until well charred and blackened in spots on all sides. Alternatively, boil the corn in salted water for 5-6 minutes until tender.
Make the dressing: While the corn grills, whisk together the mayonnaise, crema, grated garlic, and 1 tablespoon of lime juice in a small bowl until smooth. Season with a pinch of salt.

Butter the corn: As soon as the corn comes off the grill while still blazing hot, brush or rub a thin layer of butter over the entire surface. The butter adds richness and helps the mayo coating stick.
Coat with mayo: Using a brush, spoon, or your hands, coat the corn generously on all sides with the mayo-crema mixture. Don't be shy — a thick coating is key.

Add the cheese: Roll or press the cotija cheese into the mayo coating. The cheese should stick and create a dense, salty crust all around the corn. If serving on a stick, hold the stick and roll the corn in a plate of cheese.
Season generously: Dust the coated corn heavily with the chile powder and Tajín. Squeeze remaining lime juice over the top. Scatter chopped cilantro over everything.
Insert wooden skewers or corn cob holders into each ear of corn for easy street-food eating. Serve immediately while hot with extra lime, chile powder, and hot sauce on the side.

recipes.name: Breakfast Chilaquiles
recipes.description: Crispy fried tortilla chips simmered in a tangy roasted tomatillo salsa verde until they soften into layers of pure comfort. Topped with a fried egg, crema, and queso fresco, chilaquiles are the ultimate Mexican breakfast and a brilliant way to use day-old tortillas.

ingredients.name: day-old corn tortillas, cut into triangles

instructions: Fry the tortilla chips: Heat the oil in a heavy skillet over medium-high heat to 350°F. Fry the tortilla triangles in batches for 2-3 minutes, turning once, until golden and crispy. Drain on paper towels and sprinkle lightly with salt while hot. Set aside. (For a lighter version, the tortillas can also be baked at 400°F for 12-15 minutes.)

Make the salsa verde: Place the tomatillos, chiles, onion, and garlic on a foil-lined baking sheet and broil for 5-7 minutes until blistered and charred in spots. Transfer to a blender with the cilantro and a pinch of salt. Blend until smooth.

Cook the salsa: Heat 1 tablespoon of oil in a large, wide skillet over medium-high heat. Pour in the blended salsa verde — it will splatter, so be careful. Stir and fry for 5 minutes until the salsa deepens in color and flavor. Add the chicken broth and stir to combine. Reduce heat to medium.

Add the chips: Add the fried tortilla chips to the skillet with the hot salsa. Toss gently to coat each chip. Cook for just 60-90 seconds — the chips should absorb the salsa and soften slightly at the edges while still retaining a little crunch in the center. Do not overcook or they will become mush.
Fry the eggs: In a small skillet, melt butter over medium heat. Fry the eggs sunny-side up or over-easy until the whites are just set but the yolks are still runny, 2-3 minutes.

Serve immediately: Divide the chilaquiles between two plates. Slide a fried egg on top of each. Drizzle generously with Mexican crema, crumble queso fresco over the top, and garnish with onion, cilantro, and avocado.
Serve at once — chilaquiles wait for no one. Every minute they sit, they soften further. The ideal texture is the border between crispy and tender.

recipes.name: Mexican Chicken Soup
recipes.description: A humble, healing Mexican chicken soup made with bone-in chicken, chunky vegetables, fresh herbs, and a light but deeply flavored broth. Every abuela in Mexico has her version — it is the ultimate comfort food and a cornerstone of Mexican home cooking.

ingredients.name: bone-in, skin-on chicken pieces (legs, thighs, breasts)
corn on the cob, cut into thirds

instructions: Place the chicken pieces in a large stockpot. Cover with cold water (about 3 quarts). Bring to a boil over high heat, skimming off any foam and fat that rises to the surface in the first 5 minutes.
Once the broth is clear, add the onion, garlic, peppercorns, bay leaves, cilantro stems, oregano, and 1 tablespoon of salt. Reduce heat to medium-low and simmer, partially covered, for 30 minutes.
Add the carrots, celery, corn, and chayote (these take longer to cook). Continue simmering for 15 minutes.
Add the potatoes and zucchini and cook for another 15 minutes until all the vegetables are tender and the chicken is cooked through and pulling away from the bone.
Remove the chicken from the pot and let it cool for 5 minutes. Pull or shred the meat off the bones in large, rustic pieces, discarding the skin and bones. Return the shredded chicken to the pot.
Taste the broth and adjust seasoning with salt. Remove and discard the onion, bay leaves, and cilantro stems. The broth should be clear, golden, and deeply savory.
Ladle into large, deep bowls making sure each serving has a good mix of chicken, vegetables, and broth. Garnish with fresh cilantro and diced onion. Serve with lime wedges and warm tortillas.

recipes.name: Huaraches
recipes.description: Oblong, sandal-shaped masa antojitos from Mexico City, pinched to a plank shape with refried beans pressed inside the dough before cooking, then topped with carne asada or other meats, salsa, and fresh toppings. Named after the traditional Mexican sandal they resemble.

ingredients.name: carne asada (grilled skirt or flank steak), sliced thin

instructions: Make the masa: Mix masa harina, salt, and warm water together, kneading for 2-3 minutes until smooth and pliable. The dough should not crack when pressed. Cover with a damp cloth.

Stuff with beans: Divide the dough into 4 equal portions. Roll each piece between your palms into a log about 6 inches long. Use your thumb to press a channel down the center of the log. Fill the channel with a generous tablespoon of refried beans. Pinch the sides of the dough up and over the beans to enclose them, then press and shape the dough back into a smooth oblong log.

Shape into huaraches: Place the bean-stuffed dough log on a plastic-wrapped surface. Press and flatten it with your palm into an oval sandal shape — about 7-8 inches long, 3 inches wide, and 1/4 inch thick. It should be thick enough to hold the filling and toppings.

Cook on comal: Heat a dry comal or griddle over medium heat. Cook each huarache for 3-4 minutes per side until firm, lightly spotted, and the surface is dry. They should hold their shape and feel sturdy.
Griddle finish: Brush a thin film of oil on the hot comal and return the huaraches for another 1-2 minutes per side until they develop a light golden crust. Keep warm in a low oven.

Cook the carne asada: Season the steak with salt, pepper, and a squeeze of lime. Heat a cast-iron skillet or grill over high heat. Cook the steak 3-4 minutes per side for medium. Rest 5 minutes, then slice thinly against the grain.

Top the huaraches: Spread a thin layer of salsa roja over each huarache. Pile on sliced carne asada, cooked nopales, and crumbled queso fresco. Drizzle with crema and add a spoonful of salsa verde. Serve immediately.

recipes.name: Crispy Tostadas with Chicken Tinga
recipes.description: Sun-crisped or fried flat corn tortillas loaded with chipotle-braised shredded chicken tinga, refried beans, and vibrant toppings. Tinga — chicken in a smoky tomato-chipotle sauce — is one of Mexico's most versatile and beloved fillings.

ingredients.name: boneless chicken breasts or thighs, boiled and shredded

instructions: Make the tostada shells: Heat the oil in a skillet over medium-high heat to 350°F. Fry each tortilla flat (use a metal spatula to hold it down if it bubbles up) for 45-60 seconds per side until rigid, golden, and completely crispy. Drain on paper towels and salt immediately. Set aside.
Make the tinga sauce: Blend the tomatoes, chipotle chiles, adobo sauce, and chicken broth together until smooth. Set aside.

Cook the tinga: Heat 1 tablespoon of oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat. Add the sliced onion and cook for 5 minutes until softened and beginning to brown. Add the garlic and cook 1 more minute.
Pour the blended tomato-chipotle sauce over the onions. Add the oregano. Cook, stirring frequently, over medium-high heat for 5-7 minutes until the sauce thickens and darkens.

Add the shredded chicken to the sauce, tossing to coat every piece. Season with salt. Cook another 5 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the chicken absorbs the sauce and the mixture is no longer soupy. The tinga should be moist but not wet.
Assemble the tostadas: Spread a thin layer of warm refried beans on each tostada shell (this acts as the glue). Top generously with the chicken tinga.
Finish with shredded lettuce, diced tomato, a drizzle of crema, crumbled queso fresco, and sliced avocado. Add pickled jalapeños for heat. Squeeze lime over the top. Serve immediately.

recipes.name: Poblano Peppers in Walnut Cream
recipes.description: The most patriotic dish in Mexico, created by nuns in Puebla in 1821 to celebrate Independence. Roasted poblano peppers stuffed with a baroque sweet-savory picadillo of pork, dried fruits, nuts, and spices, then draped in creamy white walnut sauce and decorated with red pomegranate seeds and green parsley — the colors of the Mexican flag.

ingredients.name: peach or pear, peeled and diced

instructions: Roast the poblanos: Broil the poblanos on a foil-lined baking sheet, turning every few minutes, for 10-15 minutes until all sides are blackened and charred. Transfer to a bowl, cover tightly with plastic wrap, and steam 10-15 minutes. Peel off the skins, make a vertical slit in each pepper, and carefully remove the seeds and veins through the slit, keeping the stem attached. Pat dry.

Make the picadillo filling: Heat 2 tablespoons of oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat. Add the onion and cook 5 minutes until softened. Add garlic, cook 1 minute. Add the ground pork and cook, breaking it up, until browned all over, about 8 minutes. Drain excess fat.

Add the tomatoes to the pork, season with cinnamon, cloves, pepper, and salt, and cook 5 minutes until the tomatoes break down. Add the diced peach, apple, plantain, raisins, pine nuts, and almonds. Stir everything together. Cook on medium-low heat for another 8-10 minutes until the fruit softens and the mixture is fragrant and cohesive. Taste and adjust salt. Let cool.

Make the nogada (walnut cream sauce): The freshest walnuts make the best nogada — blanch walnuts in boiling water 2 minutes to loosen any bitter skins, then peel. Add the peeled walnuts, goat cheese, crema, and sherry to a blender. Blend until completely smooth and creamy. Season with a pinch of salt and sugar if needed. The sauce should be white and thick enough to coat the back of a spoon.

Stuff the peppers: Carefully spoon 3-4 tablespoons of the cooled picadillo filling into each roasted poblano through the slit, making them generously full but able to close back. Press the slit closed.

Plate the dish: Chiles en nogada are traditionally served at room temperature, not hot. Arrange 1 or 2 stuffed peppers on each plate. Pour the cold nogada sauce generously over each pepper so it drapes down both sides.

Garnish with pomegranate seeds and scattered fresh parsley leaves. The three colors — green pepper, white sauce, red pomegranate — represent the Mexican flag. Serve at room temperature with warm tortillas.

recipes.name: Crispy Cheese Birria Tacos
recipes.description: The modern evolution of birria — crispy, griddled tacos stuffed with slow-braised beef and molten Oaxacan cheese, with the tortilla dipped in red chile fat for a striking, deeply colored crust. Born in Tijuana street carts and made famous on social media. Served with a cup of rich consommé for dipping.

ingredients.name: beef chuck roast, cut into large chunks
dried guajillo chiles, stemmed and seeded
dried ancho chiles, stemmed and seeded

instructions: Prepare the chile sauce: Toast the guajillo, ancho, and árbol chiles in a dry skillet 30 seconds per side until fragrant. Place in a pot with the tomatoes, half the onion, and 3 garlic cloves. Cover with water, bring to a boil, simmer 10 minutes until soft. Drain, reserving 1 cup of the soaking liquid.

Blend the sauce: Transfer the chiles and vegetables to a blender with the reserved soaking liquid, beef broth, vinegar, remaining garlic, cumin, oregano, and cinnamon. Blend until completely smooth, then strain through a fine-mesh sieve.

Braise the beef: Season the beef with salt and pepper. In a large Dutch oven over high heat, sear the beef pieces in batches until deeply browned on all sides. Pour the strained chile sauce over the beef. Add bay leaves and enough water to just submerge the meat. Bring to a boil, then cover and braise on low heat for 3-3.5 hours until the beef is fall-apart tender.

Shred and reserve: Remove the beef, shred it finely, and set aside. Strain the braising liquid (this is the consommé). Skim the red chile-infused fat that rises to the top and collect it in a shallow bowl — this fat is the key to the quesabirria's famous red color and flavor.
Heat the consommé gently in a saucepan and keep warm. Season it with salt. Prepare serving cups for dipping.

Make the quesabirria: Heat a comal or large flat griddle over medium-high heat. Quickly dip a corn tortilla into the shallow dish of red chile fat, fully coating both sides, then immediately lay it on the hot comal. Add a generous handful of shredded Oaxacan cheese to one half of the tortilla, then add 2-3 tablespoons of shredded birria on top of the cheese. Fold the empty half of the tortilla over the filled half like a quesadilla.

Cook 1-2 minutes until the bottom is deeply golden and crispy, then flip and cook another 60 seconds. The cheese should be fully melted and the exterior fire-engine red and crispy. Serve immediately with cups of hot consommé, diced onion, cilantro, lime, and salsa roja.
